title: Is conservative modernism the way forward for the right?
gist: Reviewing Christos Hadjiyiannis's 'Conservative Modernists', Michael Lucchese argues that the early 20th-century Tory literary avant-garde (TS Eliot, TE Hulme, Ezra Pound, Ford Madox Ford) built a serious intellectual programme out of electoral catastrophe, and that today's Anglo-American right - dominated by demagoguery and 'AI slop' - has nothing comparable. The historical parallel is a party crushed at the polls that rebuilt itself through ideas rather than populist affect.

insights.claim: The British Conservative party lost 246 seats in the 1906 general election, a defeat severe enough that the loss itself - not policy - became the trigger for a decade of right-wing intellectual reconstruction.
insights.speaker: Michael Lucchese
insights.so_what: A template for reading parties after wipeout defeats: whether the response is intellectual reconstruction or populist affect predicts whether the party becomes governable again.
insights.quote: The Conservatives were simply incapable of competing with new modes of mass politics innovated by liberal and socialist opponents and lost 246 seats in the 1906 general election
insights.locator: What was the political context for conservative modernism?

insights.claim: Conservative modernists did not try to replace the Conservative party but to 'stiffen its spine' and consolidate its ideas - an insurgency-from-within model rather than third-party formation.
insights.speaker: Michael Lucchese
insights.so_what: Distinguishes reformers who capture an existing institution from splitters who fragment the vote - the former is historically the path back to power.
insights.quote: On the whole, they did not seek to replace the Conservative party so much as stiffen its spine and consolidate its ideas around classical modernity.
insights.locator: Although most shared this general outlook

themes.theme: Classicism vs romanticism as a political operating system

insights.claim: TE Hulme's classicism rests on a fixed-human-nature premise - that man is constant and only tradition and organisation extract anything decent from him - which is the philosophical opposite of the progress assumption underlying liberal reform.
insights.speaker: Michael Lucchese
insights.so_what: A durable lens for classifying political programmes: whether they assume human improvability (reform-heavy) or fixity (institution-heavy) drives everything downstream.
insights.quote: Man is an extraordinarily fixed and limited animal whose nature is absolutely constant. It is only by tradition and organisation that anything decent can be got out of him.
insights.locator: At the heart of this critique of liberalism

insights.claim: Classical modernism was paradoxically backward-looking - a movement that overturned romanticism while being 'full of nostalgia for a mythical past'.
insights.speaker: Michael Lucchese
insights.so_what: Aesthetic radicalism and political conservatism can be tightly coupled; do not assume avant-garde cultural production implies progressive politics.
insights.quote: As a movement that sought to overturn romanticism, classical modernism was actually full of nostalgia for a mythical past
insights.locator: Hadjiyiannis goes straight to the roots of modernist renewal

insights.claim: The conservative modernists treated the House of Lords as classicism embodied in a single institution, and Hulme defended it by analogy to the United States Senate as a check on democratic excess.
insights.speaker: Michael Lucchese
insights.so_what: Upper-chamber reform fights are proxy battles over whether elite veto points survive; the argument structure recurs wherever second chambers are attacked.
insights.locator: Perhaps the single most important controversy

insights.claim: The century-long campaign to strip the House of Lords of authority, begun after the Lords vetoed the People's Budget, has in the author's reading finally succeeded under Britain's present Labour government.
insights.speaker: Michael Lucchese
insights.so_what: A UK constitutional check widely assumed to be permanent has, on this account, been removed - relevant to how quickly future UK legislation can move.
insights.quote: a mission, it seems, that has finally succeeded under Britain's present Labour government
insights.locator: Especially after the Lords vetoed the People's Budget

insights.claim: Hadjiyiannis's diagnostic is that conservatism turns authoritarian not when it asserts external standards but when it absolutises the particular by reference only to an internal value such as the author's own conscience.
insights.speaker: Michael Lucchese
insights.so_what: A usable test for when a traditionalist political movement is about to become dangerous - watch for absolutes derived from internal conviction rather than external reference.
insights.quote: Conservatism runs the risk of becoming authoritarian not when it asserts external and irreducible standards, but when it renders things that are necessarily particular into absolutes
insights.locator: Hadjiyiannis ably addresses the danger of power politics

insights.claim: The same intellectual cohort split sharply in outcome - Hulme died in the trenches in 1917 defending liberal-order ideals while Pound drifted into fascism - showing that a shared philosophical premise does not determine political destination.
insights.speaker: Michael Lucchese
insights.so_what: Warns against treating any ideological family as having a single inevitable endpoint; personnel and circumstance matter as much as doctrine.
insights.locator: Some conservative modernists took the logic of aristocracy further

insights.claim: The conservative modernists championed abstract art - now a punching bag for the 'very-online' right - because they believed artistic freedom reconnected people to transcendence, and because they regarded boredom itself as a form of tyranny.
insights.speaker: Michael Lucchese
insights.so_what: Today's cultural right is positioned against a tradition it claims to inherit; that inconsistency is a tell about how shallow its intellectual lineage actually is.
insights.quote: Although the genre has become something of a punching bag for today's 'very-online' right, writers like Eliot and Hulme were essential to its early development.
insights.locator: To the extent Hadjiyiannis does reckon

insights.claim: Hulme defended the sculptor Jacob Epstein against antisemitic criticism by explicitly linking Epstein's art to the conservatism of Disraeli.
insights.speaker: Michael Lucchese
insights.so_what: Concrete counter-evidence to the assumption that early 20th-century literary conservatism was uniformly antisemitic.
insights.locator: Hulme was a particular defender of the sculptor Jacob Epstein

insights.claim: TS Eliot opposed centralised power under capitalism as well as socialism, finding the idea of an international 'planned economy' and 'planned culture' anathema - a liberty commitment usually credited only to liberals.
insights.speaker: Michael Lucchese
insights.so_what: Useful corrective when mapping historical right-wing thought onto today's statist-versus-market divide; the conservative modernists were anti-centralisation on both flanks.
insights.quote: TS Eliot set his face against centralized power, whether under ‘capitalism’ or some socialist regime
insights.locator: At the same time, Hadjiyiannis can sometimes over-emphasise

themes.theme: Geopolitics as a precondition for high culture

insights.claim: Hulme argued that a militarist, expansionist German state dominating Europe would mean 'the end of Europe as we know it, as a comity of nations' and result in tyranny - framing the First World War as a defence of the conditions for civilisation rather than a national interest.
insights.speaker: Michael Lucchese
insights.so_what: The argument that cultural and economic life depends on a non-revanchist regional order is recurrent and maps directly onto contemporary European security debates.
insights.quote: A German victory would signal ‘the end of Europe as we know it, as a comity of nations’ and ‘result in a tyranny’
insights.locator: The concern for liberty is also manifested

insights.claim: Across all the distinct and contradictory conservative modernisms, duty and sacrifice are the recurring higher values demanded of writer, reader, ruler and citizen alike.
insights.speaker: Michael Lucchese
insights.so_what: Identifies the specific value set the author thinks is missing from contemporary right-wing politics - a diagnostic for distinguishing serious from performative movements.
insights.quote: all of the conservative modernisms we have investigated – distinct and contradictory as they may be – elevate duty and sacrifice to higher values required for the correct function of literature and society
insights.locator: In that sense, one of the most important lessons

insights.claim: The dominant populism of both right and left today plays into vulgarity and power politics rather than defending high culture, leaving Anglo-American politics open to a party of intellectual renewal.
insights.speaker: Michael Lucchese
insights.so_what: The author is implicitly calling a gap in the political market - an intellectually serious right - which is where new political entrants historically emerge.
insights.quote: Anglo-American politics cries out for something better than the demagoguery and AI slop that now dominate right-wing discourse.
insights.locator: It is perhaps these high aims that are missed most
